conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in caring for mothers during pregnancy and after birth, so you’re in exactly the right place.

I’d like to spend a few minutes with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—often called the EPDS. It’s a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past week. It’s not a test, and there are no right or wrong answers; it simply gives us a snapshot so we can make sure you’re getting the support you need.

Everything you share is confidential, and this room is a safe space to talk honestly. We’ll go through 10 questions together; you can answer in your own words, and we’ll take it at your pace. If any question feels difficult, just let me know and we can pause.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

[sighs softly]  
I’ve laughed a few times—like when my partner made a silly face at the baby—but mostly it feels like work to crack a smile. Things that used to seem hilarious just feel kind of flat lately.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow nod]  
Yeah… I can still laugh, but it doesn’t come as easy. Most of the time I have to remind myself to lighten up, and even when I do laugh, it feels kind of forced—like I’m doing it because I should, not because it bubbles up naturally.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs a little, eyes on the floor]  
Not really… I mean, I’ll plan little things—like taking the baby for a walk or having coffee with a friend—but when the time comes I mostly feel tired or worried something will go wrong. It’s like the excitement drains out before I even get there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[quietly]  
Sometimes… like if the baby won’t settle, I catch myself thinking maybe I’m missing some cue or doing something wrong. I know I shouldn’t, but those thoughts pop in. It’s not all the time—just every now and then, and it doesn’t last long.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands]  
Yeah… a few nights a week I’ll lie there with my heart racing, running through all the “what-ifs” about the baby breathing, or whether I’m doing everything right. Nothing’s actually wrong in that moment, but my body still feels like something bad could happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[exhales slowly]  
Not full-blown panic… but sometimes, if the baby’s been crying for a while, my chest gets tight and I feel this sudden rush of “I can’t do this.” It passes pretty quickly once I get her settled, but in that moment it’s scary.
Things have been getting on top of me

[small, tired laugh]  
Most days, yeah. Between feedings, diapers, and trying to grab a shower, it feels like I’m always one step behind. I manage, but by evening I’m just… done. Some nights I look around at the mess and think, “I’ll never catch up.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[shifts in seat, eyes tired]  
A few nights this week I couldn’t fall asleep even when the baby was out. My mind just kept looping through the day—did I burp her long enough, was that rash normal… I’d lie there for an hour or two, feeling kind of sad and wound up at the same time.
I have felt sad or miserable

[quiet for a second, then nods]  
Yeah… I get waves of sadness that come and go. It’s not all day, but especially in the late afternoon or if I’m alone with the baby for a long stretch, I’ll suddenly feel weepy and heavy, like I’m missing something I can’t name.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[shakes head quickly]  
No… I haven’t actually cried. I’ve felt on the edge of tears a couple of times, but I always manage to hold them back. Crying feels like it would take more energy than I have right now.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[looks up, eyes widen]  
No—never. I could never do that to my baby or my family. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: POSTPARTUM MOOD / ANXIETY SCREENING NOTE (informal, not diagnostic)

Reported symptoms:
- Anhedonia (diminished laughter & anticipatory enjoyment)
- Intermittent low mood, “waves of sadness,” tearfulness without crying
- Recurrent self-blame regarding infant care
- Physiological anxiety (nocturnal racing heart, “what-ifs,” chest tightness)
- Episodic feeling of being overwhelmed/“can’t do this” when baby cries
- Initial insomnia (2–3 nights/week) linked to ruminative worry
- Functional impact: “always one step behind,” household tasks accumulating

Pattern: Predominantly anxious-depressive presentation, mild-to-moderate intensity, no self-harm ideation.

Screening significance: Elevated scores consistent with possible postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety; no current safety concerns.
